newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Soluble coffee imports beating beans in Ukraine.
newsitem.headline: Soluble coffee imports beating beans in Ukraine.

text.p: Imported instant coffee is gaining in popularity compared with traditionally consumed roast and ground in Ukraine's coffee market, industry and trade sources said.
"The instant coffee market is growing," said one soluble coffee importer who asked not to be identified, adding that his company expected increased sales in 1997.
"They will grow a lot," he said. "I'm not sure that we've reached market capacity yet."

Ihor Nestorovych, a manager of Videnska, a Ukrainian-Austrian joint venture importing green beans for roasting, said coffee sales had remained the same since the company started operations two years ago and were not expected to rise this year.
"We are importing about 10 tonnes of beans per month," Nestorovych said. "These are very small volumes."
He blamed a poor economy and Ukraine's wage payment crisis for lack of growth in roast coffee sales, but said forecasts for economic growth next year might improve the situation for roast.
"We are optimistic," Nestorovych said. "Right now people are not buying much. People are not being paid," he said.
He added that many Ukrainians can afford cheaper, locally-produced brands of soluble coffee or coffee substitutes.
Ukraine, with a population of 52 million people, owes about $1.5 billion to government workers, miners, students, and pensioners who have not been paid for months.
It has forecast the first economic growth next year since independence in 1991.
There are about five firms, some still state-run, which import green beans and roast them for re-sale. About three local firms manufacture soluble coffees.

Stanyslav Myronenko, chief executive of UkrKonditerProm, a state concern which imports coffee along with cocoa, nuts, and tea, said there were no changes in Ukraine's coffee imports from previous years. He did not provide figures.
"There are a lot more import brands available, and people are buying those," he said.
One industry source said the shadow economy, estimated to account for about 40 percent of all economic activity, allowed Ukrainians more purchasing power than official statistics indicated.
"Otherwise we can't explain our sales," he said.
Ukraine has traditionally consumed coffee and tea in equal amounts, and one importer said it was easier to convert tea-drinkers to soluble brands.
Brands like Nescafe, produced by Nestle SA , appear prominently in street kiosks and on the shelves of upscale supermarkets carrying imported food products.
The company has made a strong push into the Ukrainian market with advertising campaigns and free samples.
